lesson.title: The Default Verdict: Understanding the Null Hypothesis
lesson.summary: The null hypothesis, written H0, is the skeptical baseline claim of no effect or no difference in a population parameter, assumed true for the sake of argument until sample evidence says otherwise.
lesson.body:
Every hypothesis test begins with the null hypothesis, written H0, a precise statement about a population parameter (the same kind of fixed, unknown quantity you estimate with a confidence interval) claiming that nothing unusual is happening: no effect, no difference, no change from an assumed or historical value. The null hypothesis always contains an equals sign, because it stakes out one exact value for the parameter, not a range or a direction.

A few examples make the pattern concrete. Testing whether a coin is fair: H0: p = 0.5, where p is the true probability the coin lands heads. Testing whether a new medical treatment has the same recovery rate as an established treatment known to work 40 percent of the time: H0: p = 0.40. Testing whether two groups have the same underlying proportion, such as the two tutoring programs from earlier chapters: H0: p1 = p2, which can equivalently be written H0: p1 minus p2 = 0. In every case, the null hypothesis is the specific, checkable number that the test is built around, and it is exactly this claimed value that a pooled proportion, or a single hypothesized p, gets plugged into when computing a test statistic.

The name 'null' literally refers to a null, or zero, effect, the claim that whatever difference or change you might be looking for is actually absent. It is presumed true throughout the entire test, the same way a defendant is presumed innocent throughout a trial, so that the test can ask a well-defined question: if this null claim were exactly correct, how likely would it be to see sample data as extreme as what was actually observed?

A subtlety worth stating plainly: a hypothesis test never proves the null hypothesis true. The two possible conclusions are reject H0, meaning the sample data would be too surprising under H0 to be believable, or fail to reject H0, meaning the sample data are not surprising enough to abandon the null claim. Failing to reject H0 does not mean H0 has been confirmed, it only means the available evidence was not strong enough to overturn it, exactly as a not-guilty verdict does not prove innocence, it only reflects that guilt was not established beyond a reasonable doubt. With the null hypothesis defined, the next chapter turns to its counterpart, the alternative hypothesis, the claim you are actually looking for evidence of.
